text.default:
You go from house to house.

In the first there is a kitchen where somebody was in the middle of cooking, with the makings of a meal that was never finished. Nothing has rotted as it should have. It has all dried instead, as though the air in here stopped moving months ago.

The second was a family's house, and the beds still hold the shapes of the people who slept in them. In the child's room there are drawings. Most are ordinary enough, trees and animals and the village. The last few are different. The trees in them are drawn from underneath, looking up, in a light the child must have seen for themselves.

The third was an old man's house, with a writing desk covered in papers. They begin as records, the ordinary notes anyone keeps for a small village. In the last pages they become something else.
text.commander:
You find the old man's records and read them properly, in order from the beginning, watching for the point where they change.

They begin as ordinary records: harvests, births and deaths, repairs. Then the handwriting changes, and becomes a shade less careful. The entries grow shorter, and then they grow strange.
text.arcane:
The papers on the old man's desk are the most valuable thing in Harrow. You read them as carefully as you would read any original source.

There are harvest records and notes about the village, and then a register of the first signs of the curse. Somebody kept a careful account. Then, at entry 47, the account changes, and after that it is not really an account at all.
text.ranger:
The drawings in the child's room stop you short. You hold the last one up to the light.

The trees are drawn from memory, but the light is exactly right, grey and green, coming through a very thick canopy. These are not the trees at the edge of Ashenveld. They are trees from much further in.
text.cipher: You go through the houses quickly, looking for facts rather than feelings. In the third house the old man's desk is exactly what you were hoping for: the whole life and death of the village, set down on paper.

choices.text: Read all of the old man's papers.

success.text:
The last entries go like this.

Entry 51: The well tastes wrong. I have stopped mentioning it to the others.

Entry 58: Marta went to the trees this morning and came back in the afternoon. She said she just needed to think. That is probably true.

Entry 62: Joren went east and did not come back. I told myself I would go looking in the morning. In the morning I found I had other things to do.

Entry 68: I am writing this because I want to remember why it was important to write things down. I know it was important. I can feel the shape of the reason without the substance of it.

Entry 71: Tomorrow I am going to the trees. I have been going to the trees every day for two weeks. This time I will keep going. I think that is what happens next.

There is nothing after that.

success_at_cost.text: You get the general drift of it. The records are ordinary, then a little wrong, then very wrong, and then they stop. The last entries are shorter than the ones before, and get shorter still, and that tells its own story.

failure.text: The writing in the later entries is hard to make out. It changes as what it says changes, and by the end you can barely read it at all. You take the papers with you, to read later in a better light.

choices.text: Take the papers and go to the barn.

default.text: You pack up the papers to read properly later. There is more to find first.

default: The barn has a cellar, as most barns do. This one was barred from the inside. There is no lock; boxes have been stacked so as to block the door, and nobody could have stacked them like that except from within.
You move the boxes. The cellar smells of old root vegetables and of something else, a smell you will come to know later, of places where people have lived a long time in a small space.

Somebody lived down here, and not long ago, within the last month or two. They stayed on in the cellar while Harrow emptied over their head. They stayed longer than anyone, long enough to cut things into the cellar wall.
Among the marks on the wall are figures. They are small, the size of your thumb, a head and a body and no face, carved again and again, dozens of them.
text.commander:
You see at once that the carvings are a map. It is laid out as a soldier would lay one out, with the important places marked and the proportions kept true.

It is a map of the ruins, showing the parts that can be reached and the deeper parts, with points marked by small signs whose meaning you do not yet know.

Somebody surveyed the ruins thoroughly, came back to Harrow, and drew it from memory on a cellar wall before going east again.
text.arcane:
The carvings are not a map, or not only a map. They are a diagram of how the power in the ruins is laid out. Somebody who knew a great deal has set down the source of the curse, the channels it spreads along, and the places where it gathers.

You half recognise the signs. They come from a tradition older than any school still practising, older than the Covenant. Whoever made them had read the old texts and made use of what they found.
text.ranger:
The carvings are not so much a map as a set of instructions for staying alive. This place is safe and that one is not. This path keeps out of the worst of it. Here is where the ground starts to feel wrong. Here is where the animals gather.

Somebody spent time in those ruins learning how to get about in them, and then came here to write down what they had learned.
text.cipher:
The carvings are a message, though not to you in particular. They are for whoever came this way afterwards. Somebody went into the ruins, came out, went in again, and wanted somebody else to know what they had found.

You read it carefully. Some of it you understand and some you don't, but all of it matters.

choices.text: Copy the carvings into your journal, and take them with you.

success.text:
You spend the best part of an hour in the cellar with your journal and a lamp, and copy everything: every mark and every sign and every indication of direction. By the end your hand aches and the air down there has given you a headache, but you have a true copy.

You go back up to the barn to sleep. Tomorrow you go to the edge of the forest.

success_at_cost.text: You copy the parts you can read. Some of the older carvings are too worn, or too obscure, to copy properly. But you have the outline, the main features and the marked places, and that is enough to find your way by.

failure.text: There is too much of it and too little time. You copy what you can, the main landmarks and a few of the signs, but you cannot make out how they join up. You fix what you can in your memory.

choices.text: Memorise what you can and sleep. Then the forest.

default.text:
You stand in the cellar for ten minutes and look, and you fix the main features in your memory.

Then you go up and sleep in the barn.

choices.text: Shift the stacked boxes along the back wall without bringing them down.

success.text:
The boxes along the back wall are packed tight from the floor to the beam. You take them down one at a time and set them on the floor in the order they came off.

Behind the last of them is a bundle of sacking tied up with twine. There is a blanket, a tin cup and a candle end in it, and a small figure carved out of bone, no longer than your thumb, worn smooth where somebody's fingers held it.

You take the figure and leave the rest as it was.

success_at_cost.text: Two boxes come down together and you catch the second against your chest. Something inside it breaks. Behind the stack is a bundle of sacking with a blanket, a cup, a candle end and a small figure carved out of bone. You take the figure. Your arms ache all the way back to the barn.

failure.text: The whole stack goes. It comes down at once, louder than anything Harrow has heard for months, and the dust takes a long while to settle. You sit on the cellar step with your sleeve over your mouth until it does. Whatever was behind the boxes is underneath them now.

text.default:
The edge of the forest is a line.

There is no gradual change at all. On one side are the trees of Harrow, the kinds you grew up with, with the right bark and the right spaces between them. On the other side are what are, strictly speaking, trees as well, but they are wrong in several ways at once.

The bark is darker. They stand too regularly, at exactly the same distance one from the next, as if somebody had planted them rather than letting them grow. The ground beyond the line is softer than it should be in this weather. And then there is the sound.

The sound stops at the line. It is not only the birds; everything stops. The wind still moves, but it moves without a sound, and beyond that point there is such a complete absence of noise that you suddenly become aware of your own heartbeat.
text.commander:
You stand at the line and weigh it up. You know very little about the ground ahead. You have something from the cellar map, from Maret, and from the man on the road, but not enough to be sure of anything. It is enough to go on, at a risk you can accept.

You have gone into worse places knowing less, you remind yourself. You also remind yourself that in most of them you had somebody at your back.
text.arcane:
You stand at the line and read it.

It is not natural. The forest does not simply change into something else here; there is a boundary, like a wall made of nothing you can see. Whoever made it made it on purpose. The people who built the ruins knew how to raise barriers in the air itself.

The note you have felt ever since you came to Ashenveld is, at this line, a whole note at last, clear and steady. It is very nearly music, if music were something you felt in your bones.
text.ranger:
You stand at the line and look at it as you look at any ground.

You know this side and you don't know that one. It is a real boundary, not only a change in how things look. The soil is different, and the damp, and something in the air that your body notices before you do.

Your body tells you this is somewhere new, and your body is quite right.
text.cipher: You stand at the line and take stock. You have had three days in Crestfall and two on the road, and you are better prepared than most people who get this far. Whether that is enough, you will find out on the other side.

default.text:
You hear her before she means you to: footsteps on the road behind you, steady, somebody walking with a purpose and in some haste.

Maret comes out of the Harrow trees with a pack on her back. She sees you standing at the edge of the forest and does not look in the least surprised.

choices.text: Step off the road and watch who is following.

default.text:
You step back among the last of the ordinary trees and wait.

It is Maret. She comes quickly along the road with a pack on her back, and stops short of the line. She doesn't see you. She stands facing the dark trees with her hands at her sides and says something to them, too quietly for you to hear. Then she waits, as if for an answer.

Then she turns round and finds you watching.

choices.text: Cross the line, and go in alone.

default.text:
You step across the line, and the sound stops.

It is not unpleasant. It is simply complete. You take three steps into the strange forest and turn to look back at the ordinary one behind you.

Then you hear footsteps on the road.

choices.text: Walk the line for a hundred paces before crossing.

default.text:
You walk north along the edge with the ordinary trees on your left. Eighty paces along you find the first cairn: three stones, waist high, with old moss on the bottom one. There is another at a hundred and forty. Somebody has marked this line, carefully, more than once.

When you come back to the road, Maret is standing there with a pack on her back, looking at the cairn you have just left.
A moment ago you watched her talk to the trees, and she knows that you did.
She stops on the ordinary side of the line and looks at you standing in the silence. Her pack is full, and she is dressed for several days on the road.
default.else: She stops beside you, an arm's length short of the line, and looks at the trees. Her pack is full, and she is dressed for several days on the road.

default: She takes a breath. "Because I sent them in," she says. "Because for fourteen months I have been telling myself they made their own choice and I ought to respect it. And because I woke up this morning and found I could not respect it any longer."

She looks at the line. "I know this place. I have been in the outskirts. I know more about what is in there than anyone, except the people who went in and did not come back." She looks at you. "You need that. And I owe it."

default.text: She is holding the letter. "This is yours," she says. "I was wrong to keep it."

default: It is new moon tomorrow. She ought to be at the tree line by the camp.

default.text: She says "the people who went in", and never "the people who died in there". You noticed it at the camp, and she still does it.

text.commander:
"You're not a soldier," you say.

"No," she says. "But I have kept twenty-three people alive for three years in a camp beside the worst of it. I know how to manage difficult ground." She pauses. "And I know when a decision I made needs putting right."

She waits for you to make up your mind.
text.arcane:
"You made an arrangement," you say, "with whatever is in there. Doesn't that make this complicated?"

"Yes," she says. "It makes it very complicated. I am telling you so before we go in rather than after. That is as honest as I know how to be about it."

You weigh the complication against what she knows. It is not a close thing.
text.ranger:
"You'll slow me down," you say. You don't say it unkindly. It is simply true.

"Perhaps," she says. "But I know the ground inside the outskirts, and you do not. And I know..." She stops, and her face hardens a little. "I know that what is in there answers some people differently. I am one of them. Having me with you changes things."
text.cipher:
"It isn't only guilt that's brought you," you say.

She looks at you for a moment. "No," she says. "I want to know what is in there. I have lived three years next to it, and I want to know." She pauses. "That is the truth."

She has owned up to it, and you decide that counts for something.

choices.text: "Come, then. You know what you're getting into."

default.text:
She steps over the line into the forest.

The sound stops for her too. She stands in the strange silence and looks about her. She isn't afraid, you notice. It is something more complicated than fear, like a person arriving at last at a place they have thought about for a very long time.

"Stay close," you say.

"Yes," she says. And then, more quietly, "I am sorry it took me so long."

choices.text: "Go back to the camp. Your people need you."

default.text:
She looks at you. "They have Branch," she says. Then: "All right."

She takes off the pack, opens it, and hands you the most useful things in it: the food, the herbs, and some notes she has made about the outskirts.

She doesn't argue, and somehow that is worse than if she had.

"Find them," she says, and goes back the way she came. You watch her until the Harrow trees hide her.

text.default:
You go into the outskirts together. She walks a little behind you and to your left, near enough to help and far enough back not to lead.

After ten minutes she says, "I saw them go in. The last time, I mean. They had been into the outskirts twice before. The third time they went deeper, and I watched them go past the marker line."

She walks on for a while without speaking.

"They were smiling," she says. "Not as the afflicted smile. There is no warmth in that. They were smiling as people do when they have finally stopped being afraid of something."
text.commander:
"What's past the marker line?" you ask.

"The ruins proper," she says. "The old city, or what is left of it." She steps round a tree whose roots are wrong, too even on either side. "You can get through the outskirts if you are careful. Past the marker line it is different. I have never been past it."

"But they went past it."

"They went past it," she says. "Alone. I watched them go."
text.arcane:
"What was your arrangement?" you ask. It is time you knew.

She is quiet for so long that you think she will not answer. Then she says, "The curse leaves some people alone. People who stop fighting it, in a certain way. It is not giving in. It is something more careful than that. You admit that it is there."

"I admitted it. What it is, and what it does, and that it is real and is not going to stop being real. And in return..." She stops. "It leaves my people alone. They are not cured, or protected. It simply does not come for them first."

"What did it cost you?"

She is silent a long while. "I know exactly what is in the ruins," she says. "And I cannot tell anyone. When I try, the words stop."
text.ranger:
You go on together through the outskirts. She knows the ground here; you can see it in the way she walks, knowing where it will bear her weight and where it won't.

"They went in smiling," you say. "That's what you said."

"Yes."

"Was that the curse?"

She thinks about it for some time. "I do not know," she says at last. "Perhaps they found something that made going deeper seem the obvious thing to do. Or perhaps the curse made it seem obvious." She pauses. "Or both."
text.cipher:
You listen without working out what to say next.

"Did they know they might not come back?" you ask.

"Yes," she says. "We talked about it the night before."

"And they went anyway."

"And they went anyway." She is quiet a moment. "Either that was courage, or it was the curse."

"You can't tell which?"

She looks at you. "Not from here. That is why we are going in."

choices.text: Keep moving. The ruins are ahead.

default.text: You go deeper into the strange forest together. The light has changed. It is no dimmer, but it is greyer, as though the colour had been taken out of it. Behind you, through the trees, you can no longer see the ordinary forest at all.

"I did not let them," she says. "I told them where. That is different, and it is no better."

She walks on. After a while she says, "You will ask me that again. Ask me when we find them."

Behind you, a day's walk back, are Crestfall and Maret's camp, and three parties who each have their own idea of what this place is and what ought to be done about it. The letter is folded inside your coat. Whatever you managed to build in three days, you have left with the people you built it with.
default.else: Behind you, a day's walk back, are Crestfall and Maret's camp, and three parties who each have their own idea of what this place is and what ought to be done about it. There is the letter Maret would not give you. Whatever you managed to build in three days, you have left with the people you built it with.

default: Ahead are the ruins, under the dark forest, and [missing person], fourteen months gone. Somewhere ahead is the source of the curse, and the answer to what was sealed here, and why.

You stand on the threshold. You are not making up your mind; you did that long ago. You only want to be sure of where you are starting from, as people do before they go somewhere they may not come back from.
text.commander:
Your last thought before you move is the one you always have before anything that matters. You know what you are there to do, you have what you have, and to hang back now would cost more than to go on.

So you go on.
text.arcane:
You write a last entry in your journal while there is still light to write by.

The source is ahead, and the pressure grows with every step. Whatever was sealed here was sealed for a good reason. I am going in to find out what the reason was, and whether the seal can be mended.

I am also going in because someone I came back to Ashenveld for is in there, and I am not the sort of person who can leave that alone.

You close the journal and go on.
text.ranger:
You go on as you go into any country you don't know, watching everything, keeping only to the direction, and reading the ground as you walk rather than stopping to read it first.

What you came for is in there, and you are going to find it.
text.cipher:
You go over it one last time: what you know, what you don't, and what you have built in three days that may matter when you come out again.

If you come out again. You put that thought aside, for now.

You go on.

text: In the deep forest the silence is complete.

The trees here are wrong in every way. The light is wrong. The ground under your feet is wrong, too soft and too level. The air tastes like the air in a room that has been shut up for a very long time.

Somewhere in the ruins ahead somebody is waiting for you, or was waiting, or wanted you to come. Or else they wanted you to stay away, and put it in such a way that staying away was impossible. Fourteen months, and a letter, and a name at the end of a note have all been pointing you here.
You will know which it was when you find them.
